entities.name: Otto V or III, Duke of Bavaria
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Otto III, a prominent member of the powerful Wittelsbach dynasty, served as Duke of Lower Bavaria from 1290 until his death in 1312, and briefly as King of Hungary and Croatia from 1305 to 1307. His dual identity as a German prince and a claimant to the Hungarian throne placed him at the nexus of Central European dynastic politics during a period of significant fragmentation and shifting alliances in both the Holy Roman Empire and the Kingdom of Hungary. His reign in Bavaria solidified Wittelsbach control, while his Hungarian venture, though ultimately unsuccessful, underscored the enduring appeal and strategic importance of the Hungarian crown among ambitious European noble houses in the early 14th century.

Born around 1261, Otto III inherited the Duchy of Lower Bavaria jointly with his cousins Louis III and Stephen I upon the death of his father, Henry XIII, in 1290. His early ducal years were marked by internal Wittelsbach power struggles and efforts to consolidate ducal authority against the Bavarian nobility. The most dramatic phase of his career began in 1305 when, through his maternal grandfather Béla IV of Hungary, he was offered the Hungarian crown by a faction of Hungarian magnates after the extinction of the Árpád dynasty. Otto traveled to Hungary, was crowned with the Holy Crown of Hungary in Székesfehérvár on December 6, 1305, and attempted to establish his rule against the rival claimant, Charles Robert of Anjou. His efforts were hampered by a lack of consistent support and the formidable opposition of Charles Robert, leading to his capture in 1307 by Ladislaus Kán, Voivode of Transylvania, and subsequent imprisonment.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Otto III's dual role as Duke of Lower Bavaria and a claimant to the Hungarian throne positioned him at a critical juncture in Central European dynastic history, influencing the consolidation of the Angevin dynasty in Hungary and shaping Wittelsbach regional power. His actions highlighted the fluidity of medieval borders and the importance of familial claims to power.
